surface_forms: le directeur de l’hôtel de Balbec

appraisal_events.evidence: Moi qui trouvais les « enjôleuses » supérieures à toutes les clientes de l’hôtel, je me contentai de lui éclater de rire au nez ; « C’était [...] un portrait inimitable » ; « Elles étaient pourtant aussi douées qu’un poète, avec plus de modestie qu’ils n’en ont généralement » ; « Dans ces moments-là elle était vraiment céleste. »
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator turns the sisters' extravagant flattery of him — which he explicitly rejects as untruthful — into a sustained demonstration of Céleste's verbal genius, ranks the two courrières above the hotel's paying clientele, laughs in the director's face when told such company is beneath a client, and closes on an unqualified apotheosis of her name. The dominant movement of the unit is the narrator-endorsed elevation of Céleste over the social code that classes her as a servant.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Bloch baissa les yeux pour ne pas avoir l’air de reconnaître sa sœur » ; Céleste insérait des propos feints « où étaient peints malicieusement tous les défauts de Bloch ».
appraisal_events.explanation: In the closing scene Bloch is shown silently disowning his sister as she and her friend flaunt their indecency, a shamed averting of the eyes that the narration reports without mitigation; the earlier mention of Céleste's mimicry of his defects reinforces that he is the unit's standing figure of ridicule.

status_effects.explanation: The narrator credits her with a poet's gift, an inimitable portraitist's malice, and closes the paragraph by literalizing her name (« vraiment céleste »), even after conceding that her furies make her detestable.

Locally she rises above her station: preferred to every lady client of the hotel, and lent reflected standing when Françoise is impressed by her brothers' marriages into episcopal families — against the director's rebuke, which the narrator dismisses.
She shares in the narrator's admiration for the pair — the admirable theatrical masks, the poet's endowment with more than a poet's modesty — though the passage's praise centres on Céleste.

His grave lesson in propriety is met with laughter in his face and the judgment that he could not understand the narrator's reasons; the aside « Au directeur, cela n’eût rien dit » marks him as socially obtuse.
He is diminished both as the butt of Céleste's malicious mimicry and, decisively, by the cowardly lowering of his eyes rather than acknowledging his sister.

The unit ends on his torment (« j’étais torturé ») at the suspicion that the girls' obscene calls were aimed at Albertine, a closing loss of composure that outweighs the amusement of the earlier scenes.

ambiguities: The unit's most conspicuous evaluative act is Céleste's lavish praise of the narrator, but he frames it as a « portrait si peu véridique » that leaves him « anéanti » and refuses to be its beneficiary; the elevation is therefore read as landing on Céleste's inventive genius rather than on the narrator himself.

Whether Albertine is locally tainted by the closing scene is left open: the obscene language is only « peut-être » addressed to her, so the passage supports the narrator's torment without confirming any discredit to her.
